prompt.context: Your client is a pharmaceutical company that is ready to launch a new drug. It is a drug for severe asthma. It is essentially the same as what is in the market today, but it is stronger, faster, and can treat severe cases that are not properly treated with today's medicine. The drug is seen as a breakthrough. The client is planning to launch this drug in Canada.
prompt.question: How should they price the drug?

clarifying_info.q: Why are they launching this drug in Canada and not the US?
clarifying_info.a: No definitive reason provided; key contextual fact is that in Canada the government essentially runs the medical system.

clarifying_info.q: How much does today's asthma drug go for?
How do the costs of manufacturing and selling the new drug compare to the current one?
How price elastic are the Canadian customers?
clarifying_info.a: The government pays for these drugs for the elderly and poor, while insurance pays for drugs for other citizens.

framework: Identify the key decision-maker / purchaser vs. the end consumer (government vs. patient)
Benchmark against the current drug price ($5) as a floor
Determine incremental value of the new drug to the payer (government): cost savings from fewer hospital/doctor visits and reduction in pain and suffering
Assess regulatory and reimbursement environment (government-run healthcare in Canada means government sets effective price ceiling)
Propose a price that captures incremental value while gaining government acceptance

questions.prompt: Who is the effective price-setter in this market, and why does that matter?
questions.guidance: Because the Canadian government pays for drugs for the elderly and poor (and insurance covers others), the government—not individual consumers—is the effective buyer and price-setter. Individual consumer price elasticity is largely irrelevant; what matters is how much the government values the improved drug.

questions.prompt: How would you quantify the incremental value of this new drug to the government payer?
questions.guidance: Two main components: (1) Avoided medical costs — calculate the cost of hospital and doctor visits that occur when the current drug fails to treat severe cases, and estimate how many such visits the new drug would eliminate; (2) Pain and suffering reduction — difficult to quantify directly, but the government may place significant value on reducing suffering if shown compelling data. Together these form the value-based pricing ceiling.

math.setup: Incremental value = (avoided hospital/doctor visit costs per severe asthma patient per year) x (number of severe patients inadequately treated by current drug). Compare this to the $5 current drug price to derive a premium.
steps: Estimate frequency of repeat hospital/doctor visits for severe asthma patients on current drug
Multiply by average cost per visit to get annual avoided cost per patient
Aggregate across the relevant patient population
Add qualitative/estimated value for pain and suffering reduction
The sum represents the maximum willingness-to-pay of the government; anchor final price below this ceiling
math.answer: Based on available information, a price of approximately $30 was proposed as reasonable — a 6x premium over the $5 current drug, justified by significant reductions in downstream medical costs and patient suffering.

recommendation: Price the new drug at approximately $30 (roughly 6x the existing $5 benchmark), contingent on demonstrating quantifiable savings to the government payer
Build a compelling value dossier for the Canadian government showing the cost savings from reduced hospitalizations and improved outcomes for severe asthma patients
risks: Government may not accept the valuation or may negotiate a lower price given their monopsony power
Inability to quantify pain-and-suffering value may weaken the case for a large premium
Competitor drugs or substitutes could undercut the pricing logic
Regulatory approval timeline in Canada may delay launch
next_steps: Conduct a detailed health-economics study quantifying hospital/doctor visit costs avoided by the new drug
Prepare a government reimbursement submission package with clinical and economic evidence
Engage early with Health Canada and provincial formulary decision-makers to understand their valuation framework
Benchmark against similar breakthrough drug launches in other government-payer markets
